If you are working toward American AAdvantage elite status this qualification year, you may be looking for more ways to earn Loyalty Points to secure your desired status. Here's what you need to know about AAdvantage elite status requirements and five ways to close your Loyalty Point gap before the end of February.

The status qualification year for American AAdvantage elite status runs from March 1 to the end of February. You need the following number of Loyalty Points to qualify for each status tier:

Your Loyalty Points reset to zero each year on March 1. However, once you earn AAdvantage elite status, you'll keep it through March 31 of the year following the end of your qualification year.

Related: American AAdvantage miles vs. Loyalty Points: What's the difference?

Loyalty Points are the sole metric for AAdvantage elite status. As a reminder, you generally earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile you earn, including miles earned through flights, credit card spending and select partners.

However, some AAdvantage miles — including those earned through credit card welcome offers and certain promotional bonuses — don't earn Loyalty Points.

Related: The best American Airlines Loyalty Point Rewards at every milestone

Here are five straightforward ways to earn more Loyalty Points before the current elite qualification year ends on Feb. 28.

You can earn Loyalty Points on eligible flights with American Airlines and its partners. Flights marketed by American and select partners, including British Airways and Iberia, earn 5 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on eligible fares, plus elite status bonuses. Other partners, including Alaska Airlines, Finnair and Japan Airlines, award Loyalty Points based on fare class and distance flown.

Basic economy tickets usually don't earn Loyalty Points.

If you have the (see rates and fees), you can also earn 5,000 bonus Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to three times per qualification year.

Related: How to earn American Airlines AAdvantage miles

You can earn Loyalty Points by shopping through the AAdvantage eShopping portal or using eligible SimplyMiles offers with an enrolled Mastercard. However, Loyalty Points generally won't post until the qualifying transaction is completed and processed, which may be long after you purchase back-ordered items and hotel stays.

Related: Earn points, miles or cash back: How to maximize online shopping portals for your purchases

When you book your stay through AAdvantage Hotels, you can earn up to 15,000 Loyalty Points per reservation once you complete your stay. However, keep in mind that you usually won't get hotel elite status earning or benefits when you book through AAdvantage Hotels.

Related: How I earned 29,000 Loyalty Points and 23,000 AAdvantage miles on a single $800 hotel stay

You can earn Loyalty Points at participating AAdvantage Dining restaurants. Just be sure to register your favorite dining rewards cards in the AAdvantage Dining program — which will unregister them from most other dining rewards programs — and then use an enrolled card to pay at participating restaurants.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

You can also earn Loyalty Points when you use AAdvantage credit cards for purchases. Specifically, you'll generally earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent on eligible purchases with an AAdvantage credit card, regardless of whether the card earns bonus miles in certain spending categories. Purchases made through Feb. 28, 2027, will earn Loyalty Points that count toward the status qualification year ending on Feb. 28, 2027, even if your statement closes in March.

The (see rates and fees) also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds — 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points — for up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per qualification year. These thresholds include Loyalty Points earned through all eligible methods, not just card spending.

Related: Which AAdvantage card is right for you? Here are 3 options you should consider

American AAdvantage has yet to announce whether it will change its elite status tiers or qualification requirements for the next qualification year, which will run from March 1, 2027, to Feb. 29, 2028.

If you're short on Loyalty Points for your desired AAdvantage elite status, you still have time to close the gap before Feb. 28, 2027. Whether you fly, shop, dine, book hotels or spend on an AAdvantage credit card, be sure to understand when your activity will count toward status qualification.

#6207. Headed to Puerto Rico? These Beaches Belong on Your Bucket List

My father grew up on Puerto Rico's west coast, where beach days began with a barefoot walk to the sand around the neighborhoods of Isabela or Aguadilla and often ended wherever the waves happened to be breaking next. I grew up on stories of salty hair, sun-warmed sand, and long, glittering afternoons in the water. Eventually, I started following in his footsteps, exploring the island’s beaches for myself and discovering just how many different shades of paradise fit along its 300 miles of coastline. There are the rollicking Atlantic surf breaks at Jobos and Middles, the impossibly blue waters and colorful fishing boats of Crash Boat, the mangrove-fringed coastline around La Parguera, and the powdery white sands of Culebra's Flamenco Beach. Some days call for a boat ride out to Culebrita’s secluded Tortuga Beach; others are better spent under the palms in Luquillo, with a plate of fresh seafood and a cold Medalla from the nearby kiosks.

The island is filled with beaches, all with a slightly different personality. Whether your plan is to wake up early and arrive with a surfboard, head out on a boat ride, snorkel, or lounge on the sand with absolutely no plans at all, I've got a rec for you. From well-loved surf towns to far-flung island hideaways, these are the best beaches in Puerto Rico worth building a trip around—plus, where to stay when you get there.

Head to dreamy Playa Jobos (or Jobos Beach)…

…for local vibes, sublime swells, a colorful coast

Head to Culebra, a lush island off the east coast, and you'll find Flamenco Beach, a gorgeous white-sand beach that's just over one mile long. It sits inside a broad, horseshoe-shaped bay, where the curve of the land shields the coastline from heavy Atlantic swells, so the water remains calm and clear for long stretches. The layers of color can be seen overhead: pale green near the shore, then deeper blue as the floor drops away. A quintessential tropical beach, the sand here is as fine as flour, remarkably pale and cool. While the shore is relatively short, it is wide enough that you can always find a spot to claim as your own, even on busy peak weekends.

Not to mention, the beach was ranked one of the top 50 beaches in the world for 2026—the Caribbean gem landed the 41st spot globally and 10th in North America on The World’s 50 Best Beaches list for 2026.

Jobos Beach is one of those stretches that captures the easygoing, salt-in-your-hair spirit of Puerto Rico’s northwest coast. Tucked into Isabela’s Bajuras neighborhood, the sandy bay is framed by a rocky headland, with a well-known reef break that draws local surfers and visiting wave-chasers alike. Even if you don't surf, there's plenty to keep you busy here: watch the lineup from the shore, book a lesson with Moku Surf Shop, or settle in at one of the beachside restaurants next door for fresh seafood and a table with an ocean view. The surrounding stretch of coast is dotted with little places to eat and drink, so it's easy to make an afternoon of it, whether you're coming straight from the water or just looking for a laid-back lunch with a view. Jobos is a proper surf beach, though, not a reliably calm swimming cove; strong currents and changing conditions are part of the picture, so take care before heading in.

The path to this beach is a bit of a trek: Starting in Ceiba, a small town to the northeast of the main island, travelers will need to take a ferry to Culebra followed by another 30-minute boat ride via water taxi or tour group to Culebrita (little Culebra). But trust that the ride is well worth the reward of unspoiled paradise—it's even sea-turtle-approved. The beach's name Tortuga nods to the herds of turtles that visit its shores from February to August and make for superb snorkeling companions. Above water, the beach welcomes a Robinson Crusoe variety of fun with its lush untamed jungles and powder-soft white sands. Make sure to grab everything you'll need for a few hours of fun—because of Tortuga's removed location, you won't find amenities like bathrooms or food stands close by.

The piers here were initially built so the US military could quickly recover downed airmen from Ramey Air Force Base, thus explaining the name, “Crash Boat Beach.” Located on the west side of the island in Aguadilla, this beach's past life as a military outpost feels far behind it—dinghies and fishing boats of all shapes, shades, and sizes line the highlighter-painted piers and the unofficial soundtrack of the shore comes from the speakers and boomboxes pulsing to reggaeton beats. Whether you're here to party at some of the best bars in Puerto Rico or enjoy the calmer life that carries on at sea, visitors are welcome to take their sweet time here, thanks to the well-stocked kiosks of water sports pavilions, umbrella rentals, and food stands, selling any wares you might need for a long day at the beach.

A one-mile crescent that arcs along the island's northern coast, Pine Grove provides a taste of the Atlantic's stronger waves, making it one of Puerto Rico's most popular surf spots for those just starting out. Especially during the month of December, the east side of this beach tends to catch consistent three-to-four-foot swells, making it a great place for beginners to learn how to surf. The convenient location is a welcome bonus; as a beach in Isla Verde, Pine Grove is a mere five minutes away from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), so you can hit the sands as soon as you're wheels down in the Caribbean.

Where to stay near Pine Grove Surfing Beach:

Vieques is a six-mile skip to the southeast of the main island, and once dubbed, “La Isla Nena” by Puerto Rican poet Luis Llorens Torres—this island plays the role of darling little sister perfectly. And where better to experience the island's charms than on one of its beaches? La Chiva is a part of the Vieques National Wildlife Refuge, where a few steps to your left may lead you to a forest of mangroves, a few to the right, a stunning coastal lagoon. Take it all in surrounded by the friendly company of wild horses, sea turtles, manatees, and diving seabirds. Stretching out for one and a half miles, this is a leisurely walk along the beach that's begging to be taken. If you're enticed to do more in the clear-as-glass turquoise waters, head off to nearby Chiva Bay, one of the best snorkeling spots in Puerto Rico.

Also known as Balneario La Monserrate, Luquillo Beach is so much more than its 12 miles of golden sands, tranquil waters, and fanning palms—though all of the above are fabulous. The beach borders El Yunque National Forest, the only rainforest registered in the US National Parks system. If you're searching to pack your itinerary with more than swimming, surfing, and snorkeling, head for the mountains: For can't-miss sights, journey up the main road to La Coca waterfall for a cool mist and Yokahú Tower, an observation tower where you can behold the entire forest floor before you.

Technically, La Parguera has no beaches. But you won't miss any other shores after spending a day at these cays. Rent out a small boat or book with a local tour operator to explore the mild seas. Cays like Mata La Gata have shaded picnic areas for a casual lunch in paradise, while the gin-clear waters at Cayo Caracoles have natural walking paths lined with mangroves. Pressed for time and only able to visit one? Plan an after-hours trip to La Parguera's bioluminescent bay—one of three in Puerto Rico, and the only one visitors are permitted to swim in—which lights up an electric blue as you swim through the clouds of plankton that sparkle like glitter against the dark blue water.

This is one for the snorkelers. For a strong chance of seeing bus-sized manta rays, sea turtles, and marine life in every other form and flavor, look no further than in Tamarindo's welcoming waters. For those who aren't looking to paddle too far, the serene ocean in these parts is ideal for young families and those of all ages who'd rather just dip their feet in. While the entertainment and dining scene is virtually nonexistent, the opportunities for relaxation and reconnecting with nature are unparalleled.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6206. Air Algerie Business Class Airbus A330neo Review: Utterly Awful

For the first long haul segment of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class on the 6hr50min flight from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG). I had heard almost entirely negative things about Air Algerie, which intrigued me, naturally! Well, now that I’ve flown Air Algerie I can confirm that everything I heard was true, and then some.

I don’t want to be dramatic — obviously flying business class is better than economy — but honestly, just about everything sucked. On the plus side, the seats as such were fine, but that’s where the good news ends. The food was not good, and took an insanely long amount of time to be served. There were no amenity kits… or menus… or meal choice… or alcohol… or diet soda. If the crew were any more indifferent, they would’ve been invisible.

I wouldn’t fly Air Algerie again unless I absolutely had to, which… I can’t imagine that’ll ever be the case. Honestly, Air Algerie made me yearn for my recent flight on Turkmenistan Airlines, which was at least fun.

Air Algerie is a pretty isolated airline, which perhaps reflects Algeria overall — the country just isn’t interested in visitors, and getting a visa requires jumping through hoops.

So Air Algerie doesn’t have any useful partnerships when it comes to earning or redeeming miles. As a result, booking a cash ticket is just about the only option, unless you’re a frequent flyer with the airline. Air Algerie tends to have rather steep business class fares, despite its lackluster product.

However, I did manage to find a rather attractive one-way business class fare. I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

The first segment was operated by an Airbus A330-900neo, while the second segment was operated by an Airbus A320 that was wet leased from Avion Express.

I had flown into Montreal the same day from Miami (MIA) on Air Canada Rouge, so I had an extended layover. I was at the Air Algerie check-in counter before it opened at 12:30PM, and there was already quite the queue of passengers waiting. Unsurprisingly, and as is very common for North Africa flights, people had a ton of checked bags.

It took me around 30 minutes to get checked in, since there was one counter for business class, and there were half a dozen people in front of me. At first I was asked if I had a visa for Algeria, though I explained I was in transit, which seemed to catch the check-in agent off guard. Air Algerie is clearly targeted at the local community, and doesn’t see much international connecting traffic.

Security was a breeze, and Air Algerie sends its business class passengers to the National Bank Lounge, which is the contract lounge in the international portion of the terminal. I won’t do a full review, but it was actually a pretty pleasant facility, with plenty of seating, lots of natural light, and it wasn’t very crowded.

The food selection was pretty average, with a handful of hot options, plus cheese, cold cuts, etc. There was coffee, tea, wine, beer, and soft drinks. I made the mistake of saving my hunger and thirst for onboard the Air Algerie flight!

My Air Algerie flight was departing from gate A58, with boarding scheduled for 3:10PM, a full hour before departure. I was at the gate early enough to see the inbound aircraft arrive, and goodness, what a stunner it was!

The Montreal route is primarily served by an A330neo with the registration code 7T-VLB, which is in a special livery celebrating the country’s football team. Looking at the plane was honestly the best part of the flight experience, unfortunately.

The boarding area got very full before departure, with lots of passengers in wheelchairs, and lots of crowding around the gate. Boarding ended up starting at 3:20PM, with those needing extra time, as well as business class passengers, being invited to board first.

I can’t describe how excited I was to step onboard, as I always love trying new airlines! I wasn’t fully prepared for the level of indifference shown by every part of the experience, though.

Before I get into this review, I should mention that Air Algerie has recently started taking delivery of Airbus A330-900neos as part of its fleet modernization initiative. However, the airline isn’t just taking delivery of these planes factory fresh, but has also acquired a couple secondhand from Air Belgium, which went out of business in 2024.

Air Algerie maintained the Air Belgium interiors — they also have staggered seats, but it’s a slightly different configuration. I boarded through the second door on the left, and then turned left into the business class cabin.

Business class takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors, and consists of 30 seats, spread across eight rows, in a 1-2-1 configuration. These seats are from the Stelia Aerospace Solstys line, so they’re typical last generation staggered business class seats. When it comes to the seat details, they have 44″ of pitch, 21″ of width, and convert into 77″ flat beds.

On the plus side, it’s really easy to photograph Air Algerie cabins, since crews are nowhere to be seen. 😉

If you’re traveling with someone, you may appreciate the sets of center seats in odd numbered rows, as these are “honeymoon” seats, which allow you to sit really close to your companion. Meanwhile in even numbered rows, the seats in the center section are further from one another and really close to the aisles, so those would be my least preferred seats in this configuration.

Along the windows, seats alternate between being closer to the aisle and closer to the windows. In odd numbered rows, seats are closer to the aisle. What I particularly don’t like about these staggered seats is just how exposed some of them are to the aisle, as you really have no separation.

In even numbered rows, seats are closer to the windows, and these are the best seats in the house, in terms of offering some separation from the aisle, and an easy view out the window.

I assigned myself seat 6A, the window seat on the left side in the third to last row.

These staggered seats have a console to the side of the seat, and on the side of that is a panel with seat controls, an entertainment controller, and a small armrest.

There’s an exposed storage area above the panel, where you can store things, or even hang the headphones. As you can see, the seat just wasn’t well maintained, and also wasn’t clean, as it also needed a good wiping down.

In terms of charging, the AC power outlet and USB-A outlet were located underneath the seat. There was no USB-C or wireless charging, unsurprisingly.

Looking at the front of the seat, the tray table is stored behind the seat in front, and can be extended by being lowered and then moved over. One of the nice things about these tray tables is that you can angle them away from you, so it’s possible to get up during the meal service.

The entertainment system is in a fixed position and is located above the ottoman. The monitor here was 16″ and was touchscreen, but wasn’t terribly high definition.

As much as there are many aspects of this seat I don’t love, I do like how big the footwell is, which is great for those of us with big feet. It’s not necessarily that comfortable when you’re laying sideways in terms of space for knees, but still, there was a great amount of space here.

One other interesting note is that there were no overhead bins in the center of the cabin, so the overhead bins along the windows got pretty full, since the A330neo doesn’t have huge bins. On top of that, there were no individual air nozzles above seats, sadly. That was a problem on this flight, given how warm the cabin was kept.

All-in-all, Air Algerie’s business class hard product is okay. The cabin maintenance could definitely use some help, but honestly, this is the least of Air Algerie’s problems.

The Air Algerie business class entertainment system on the A330neo is pretty awful. For one, there’s not even a map feature. I’m sorry, I’m not sure the last time I flew an airline with seat back entertainment that didn’t have a map feature. What’s going on there?

The system did have some movies, TV shows, and music, but it was a really lackluster selection.

In total, there were 100 movies and 36 TV shows, but it definitely felt like the number of “popular” options was limited.

The airline presumably went with the cheapest entertainment package available. For example, when it comes to sitcoms, there was one episode of “Fresh Off The Boat,” and it was the pilot episode from 2015. Yikes.

When it comes to Wi-Fi, that’s something that just isn’t offered by Air Algerie. Funny enough, these ex-Air Belgium A330neos have Wi-Fi installed, but the airline just chooses not to use the system. So expect that you’re going to disconnect when flying with Air Algerie.

When it comes to amenities in Air Algerie business class, they were also very limited. The highlight was the pillow and blanket, which were at the seat upon boarding, but not exactly very nicely presented.

Anyway, this was the highlight of the amenities, and while they were nothing amazing, they were at least decent.

Headphones were also passed out well after takeoff, though the quality of them was very poor. This was closer to what you’d expect in economy than business class.

There were no amenity kits, or anything else to speak of. I don’t remember the last overnight business class flight I’ve taken where I wasn’t offered an amenity kit?

Despite the very drawn out boarding process, the crew was nowhere to be seen for most of boarding. Finally at 4:10PM, right at departure time, they came around with pre-departure drinks. There was no “hello” or “welcome onboard,” but instead, just the tray being held out with orange juice or water. At least it was served in glassware… yay?

Boarding this Air Algerie A330neo took an incredibly long time. Every seat was taken (business class seemed to be occupied mostly by operational upgrades plus friends and family). There was just endless confusion, and the crew’s only involvement with things was to occasionally check on people they knew and have chats with them, while everyone else was ignored.

Boarding was also rough because it seemed like the APU was broken, so the cabin was incredibly hot. During boarding, I had asked the flight attendant if I could use the lavatory (I try to do that as a courtesy, even though it showed as unoccupied), and she responded “wait.” I checked with her again some time later, and she again said “wait.” I didn’t end up getting to go before departure… oh well!

Our departure time came and went, and about 20 minutes later I asked a flight attendant if we were delayed. She didn’t understand my question, but after rephrasing, her answer was “no.” The door ended up closing at 4:35PM, 25 minutes behind the scheduled departure time.

At that point the manual safety demonstration began, which was exclusively performed in French and Arabic, and not in English. In fairness, I was probably the only person onboard who didn’t have French or Arabic as my first language. I should also mention there were no safety checks during taxi — some people had their seats reclined, plenty of people still had their (glass) pre-departure beverages, and the guy across from me didn’t even have his seatbelt on.

We began our pushback at 4:40PM, and then at 4:50PM we began our taxi.

While taxiing (and turning a corner), the captain made his welcome onboard announcement at 4:55PM, telling us “this is captain, good morning, taking off shortly.” Okay, we’ll ignore the “morning” part (I’ll assume it just means he’s well rested!), but I assume at Air Algerie the captain is also the one taxiing, right? If so, that’s a lot of multitasking, especially when you’re actively turning.

But hey, credit where credit’s due, this guy was good at turning corners. When we got to runway 24R at 5PM and were cleared for takeoff, we didn’t slowly make the turn and then accelerate. Instead, we started accelerating pretty aggressively in our turn, and were going over 15 knots, while turning at a 90 degree angle. Seriously, check the Flightradar24 data.

We had a very powerful takeoff roll and the captain pulled up on the sidestick as if we were in a fighter jet. The views on the climb out were gorgeous — what a lovely afternoon!

We made a sharp turn after takeoff, and had some nice views of the airport thanks to that.

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. A little while later, we started to get a beautiful sunset view as well.

Dinner was served after takeoff in Air Algerie business class, but my gosh, what a bad and drawn out meal it was. I can deal with bad food or slow service, but bad food, bad drinks, and slow service? BLEH. The first thing to understand is that there were no menus or choices. You’re just served stuff, and it’s a “take it or leave it” situation.

Service began 50 minutes after takeoff, when warm towels were distributed.

Then around 15 minutes later, tablecloths were handed out. These felt more like large, flimsy napkins, than actual tablecloths, but whatever, no biggie.

Another 10 minutes later, the first course was served. The actual food was a little smoked salmon, some egg, some olives, etc. It didn’t taste good at all, but what was worse was the presentation. It’s as if they just threw a bunch of packaging on the tray, and put zero effort into how it’s presented.

I couldn’t help but do their job for them, and make it look a little nicer, because it’s just embarrassing. Oh, and bread is just served by hand out of the basket. Nice.

I kind of loved the Air Algerie branding on the cutlery, but that’s the same cutlery you have to use for the entire meal. For that matter, the cutlery was downright sticky when I removed it from the packaging, so clearly it just hadn’t been cleaned properly.

Drinks were brought out separately from the meal, but they might as well not have bothered. I didn’t realize that Air Algerie is a “dry” airline — it hadn’t even made my list of airlines that are dry. As it turns out, this is only a fairly recent development, as the airline switched to being dry a few years ago.

It’s not only that they don’t have alcohol, but they don’t even have any diet sodas. They have juice or full calorie soda. There was also a huge language barrier here:

“Drink?”“Do you have wine?”“Soda, juice.”“Do you have Diet Coke?”“Coke?”“No, Diet Coke.”“What?”“Coke Zero? Diet Pepsi? Pepsi Max?”*stares blankly*“I’ll have a water, please.”*serves me Sprite*

Another 15 minutes later the main course was served. Again, there was no option, and it seemed to be some sort of a swordfish, or something. As someone who typically loves fish (and orders it way too often on planes), I found this to be way overcooked, dry, and completely tasteless. If you’re not going to offer people a choice of meals, what a random thing to serve!

After an additional pause, the crew came around with cheese plates. I mean, they certainly serve quite a quantity of food, the issue is just that there are no choices, and none of it is actually good. They also don’t actually clear any plates. They just keep bringing more and more food, and if your tray is overflowing, so be it (for the below picture, I had placed the other stuff from the tray over on the side console).

Next up, two whole apples were served, which… I mean, I can’t blame them for the excessive amount of food, serving cheese, fruit, and dessert. But still, this very much feels like an afterthought. I also couldn’t help but wonder if those apples had been washed, given that we’re talking about an airline that serves bread by hand.

Lastly there was a little dessert tart trio. I tried to order a tea without caffeine, but that was a challenge:

“Coffee or tea?”“Do you have any tea without caffeine?”“Coffee or tea?”“Tea please, but no caffeine.”“Coffee?”“Tea, please.”

The entire meal service took close to three hours. Nothing about it was good. The food wasn’t good. The service was terrible. I mean, everything was just so poorly timed. There was never even the offer for more drinks (even just bottled water), and when I did ask, it took them 15 minutes and multiple reminders to actually get some more water.

I just don’t get it. As another example, they served the cheese plates, and then 10 minutes later they came around with more bread, after just about everyone had finished their cheese course. I’m exhausted writing about this. I need a drink.

The Air Algerie A330neo business class lavatory is located at the very front of the cabin. One lavatory really isn’t enough for a full business class cabin plus the crew, so there was often a wait. While there are two lavatories behind the cabin, they’re shared with economy passengers, so there’s usually a line.

The lavatories were fine. Toward the end of the flight they definitely weren’t clean, but to be honest, I’ve seen much worse lavatories on airlines in the region, so I’m hardly going to complain.

By the time the meal service was complete, we had well under four hours remaining to Algiers. So I reclined my seat into bed mode, and tried to get a bit of rest. The bed was okay, and again, compared to the rest of the experience, it was one of the better things.

The issue is how hard it was to actually get rest on this flight. The lights were fully on until after the meal service was complete, so at that point it was under four hours until our arrival in Algiers.

Then the cabin lights were once again fully turned on exactly two hours before arrival. So for those keeping track at home, on a 6hr50min flight, the lights were dimmed for around 1hr50min. I’m not sure I actually slept for a minute. The cabin was really warm, and with the lack of individual air nozzles, I just couldn’t get comfortable.

It absolutely boggles my mind why the crew has to start the pre-landing service a full two hours before landing, when the extent of the breakfast is a single tray with a small side of fruit, a small piece of cake, and a croissant. Seriously, this is what everyone is being woken up two hours before landing for?!

Credit where credit’s due, the drip coffee with milk was drinkable, and perhaps the culinary highlight of the flight. Getting a refill was beyond my abilities, but I sure did savor that one cup!

I understand that North African countries are often known for warm hospitality in a non-transactional setting, where there’s a genuine warmth and generosity to hospitality. Clearly that doesn’t apply in a transactional setting, though, and certainly not on Air Algerie.

I don’t want to say the crew was rude — that wouldn’t be fair, and I didn’t even communicate with them enough to draw that conclusion. They actually seemed to be very nice in how they chatted with their friends who were in the cabin.

As a customer, though, everything about the service was terrible. The crew had no warmth, no attentiveness, they were incredibly disorganized and slow, and the service flow just made no sense. If I were to train a crew on how to provide good service in business class, I’d have them experience this flight, and then have them do exactly the opposite. I think I’ve ragged on them enough.

You’ve gotta love how the refreshing towel has Air Algerie’s logo, and then says “Always caring for you.” If this is what care looks like, I’d love to see what not being cared for looks like!

I was excited when my Air Algerie flight was slowly coming to an end. At around 4:20AM Algiers time the seatbelt sign was turned on, and the crew prepared the cabin for landing. Now, that didn’t actually involve doing any security checks, but they made sure passengers were aware there would be no more service.

We ended up touching down at 4:50AM, and it must’ve been one of the smoothest touchdowns of my life, as you could barely feel it. From there, we had a short five minute taxi to a remote stand, where we pulled in at 4:55AM.

It’s very odd how an airport that has so many empty gates and that’s rather underutilized sends its “flagship” aircraft to remote stands, but whatever.

Upon deplaning, there wasn’t so much as a “goodbye” from the crew. There also wasn’t any priority deplaning for business class, or a separate business class bus. It was quite a long drive to the terminal, and we got there at 5:15AM, where my interesting transit experience started…

I highly recommend flying Air Algerie business class… if you want to be reminded how every other airline doesn’t actually suck that much, by comparison. Air Algerie’s A330neo business class hard product is okay, and is the least of the issues.

The problem is everything else, from the completely indifferent crew, to the unnecessarily drawn out service, to the lack of meal options, amenity kits, menus, diet soda, alcohol, etc., to the subpar entertainment and lack of Wi-Fi… the list goes on and on. And that says nothing of the bizarre elements of the flight, like no English safety demos, no safety checks before takeoff or landing, etc.

What’s sad is that I would’ve actually had a more favorable impression of the flight if they just said “this is a sleeper flight, and we have no inflight service.” Truly, no service would’ve been better than this. I’m happy I had the chance to fly Air Algerie, but you know, I think I’m good for the time being!

What do you make of Air Algerie’s business class?

#6205. Frontier Begins First Class Ticket Sales

Frontier on Tuesday opened reservations for its upcoming First Class, which is set to debut in March 2027.

The new seats have up to 37 inches of pitch, the carrier said, and will be arranged in a two-by-two configuration at the front of the cabin. Installations are already underway. Reservations are available now for travel beginning March 5.

Frontier first announced plans to add a First Class product in late 2024.

The airline will also add extra-legroom seating, with up to 34 inches of pitch, in rows three through eight. These seats will be available with Frontier’s Premium bundle, which includes a carry-on bag and priority boarding.

Frontier plans to roll out two additional perks through 2027 – in-seat USB-C power at every seat in the first eight rows, and Starlink wireless internet service. The carrier decided on Starlink in July; it will be the first airline in the U.S. to use a new system managed directly by Starlink, officials said at the time.

“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” Bobby Schroeter, chief marketing officer at Frontier, said in a news release. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power, and fast, reliable Starlink Wi-Fi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us.”

#6204. Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card Review: Strong Bonus Categories, Weak Overall Value

Both American Express and Chase issue co-branded Marriott credit cards, meaning consumers have lots of options to choose from. This is my Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card review, as I’d like to take a look at whether this Marriott credit card is worth it.

Personally I don’t think that the Bonvoy Bevy Card is Marriott’s most compelling credit card option, and given how the offers on some cards are mutually exclusive, I think there’s a better strategy. However, everyone should decide for themselves, based on their own situation. Let’s look at the value proposition of the Bonvoy Bevy Card, including the welcome offer, annual fee, return on spending, and perks, so you can make your own decision.

Link: Learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

Before I get into the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card review, let me give you a high-level summary of the card’s main features and perks:

I also put together my list of the top pros and cons for the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card:

When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are major factors that people consider. After all, this determines how much value you can get upfront, and also how much this card will cost you in the long run. With that in mind, let’s take at the bonus and fee details for the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card currently has a welcome offer where you can earn 85,000 Bonvoy bonus points after spending $5,000 within the first six months. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Bonvoy points are worth 0.7 cents each, meaning I value the welcome offer at $595.

This is the standard welcome offer on the card, though we’ve definitely seen better bonuses in the past. For example, in the past I recall seeing a bonus of up to 125,000 points plus a $150 statement credit upon completing minimum spending. So it could be worth waiting to apply to see if a higher offer comes back around.

If applying for the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card, Amex’s general application restrictions apply, and on top of that, there are some additional restrictions for Marriott credit card eligibility.

The most important thing to understand is that you are eligible for this card, including the welcome offer, if you have the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more). However, you aren’t eligible for the welcome offer if you have the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more).

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card has a $250 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and you can add authorized users at no extra cost.

Among Marriott personal credit cards, this card has the second-highest annual fee (there are also no annual fee and $95 annual fee options), with the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) being the only card with a higher annual fee — it has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees).

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card is supposed to be the best credit card for actually earning points, so the card has a pretty decent rewards structure. The card offers the following return on spending, all with no foreign transaction fees:

Ultimately these are just about the best bonus categories you’ll see on a co-branded Marriott credit card. However:

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers a variety of perks for being a cardmember. Some perks are offered just for having the card, while other perks require spending or other activity. Let’s go over the details, in no particular order.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers 1,000 bonus points per paid eligible stay with Marriott, which is a perk that’s unique to this card. You need to pay for your stay with the card to be eligible, and only paid stays booked directly with Marriott qualify (so third party bookings and award stays don’t count). Bonus points will post within six weeks of an eligible stay.

For the very frequent Marriott guest, this has the potential to be pretty useful, especially if you make frequent, short stays. Based on my valuation of Bonvoy points, this is like an incremental return of roughly $7 per paid stay.

Unfortunately, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card doesn’t offer a free night award just for being a cardmember. Rather, you can earn a free night award valid at a property costing up to 50,000 points when you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

It’s also possible to top off Marriott free night awards with up to 25,000 additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. This means you could redeem a free night award plus 25,000 points to stay at a hotel costing 75,000 points per night.

This is a disappointing aspect of the card, as several other Marriott credit cards don’t require you to spend any amount to earn such a certificate.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers complimentary Marriott Bonvoy® Gold Elite status for as long as you’re a cardmember. This is better than nothing, but don’t get too excited. Marriott Gold status offers perks like:

Just for having the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card you receive 15 elite nights toward status annually. This can help you if you’re looking to earn a higher elite tier, like Marriott Bonvoy® Platinum Elite status, Titanium Elite status or Ambassador Elite status, and it can also help you with earning Choice Benefits (like Nightly Upgrade Awards).

It’s also worth noting that you can stack the 15 elite night credits on this card with elite night credits earned on a Marriott business credit card. That gets you a long way toward the Marriott Bonvoy Platinum Elite status requirement of 50 nights.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers some extra protections both when you’re traveling and making purchases with your card. These include:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Looking at the card in isolation, there’s a case to be made for getting the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card, especially if you’re a very frequent Marriott guest. If you put all your Marriott spending on the card, you’d earn 1,000 bonus points per stay, 6x points on Marriott spending, and you could earn a free night award after spending $15,000.

But even if you’re set on a Marriott credit card, there are better options, as I view it, especially given how some cards are (somewhat) mutually exclusive, at least when it comes to welcome offers.

If you ask me, the Bonvoy Bevy Card is the weakest card in the Marriott credit card portfolio in terms of value for the annual fee, and I think you’re much better off going for the higher annual fee card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card (learn more) has a $650 annual fee, and offers:

As I see it, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card’s annual fee easily pays for itself, between the dining credit, anniversary free night award, elite status, Priority Pass™ membership, and more.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card (learn more) has a lower annual fee of $95, but in my opinion it offers significantly more value than the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card. Its perks include:

The free night award alone makes this card worth it. You get this once every account anniversary year, and you can top off the free night with an additional 25,000 points. Even though the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card’s free night award is valid for rooms that cost up to 50,000 points, it’s not worth spending $15,000 on the card in a year just to earn it.

If you’re not actually that committed to the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem, there are lots of other great cards to consider. In particular, these are cards with relatively reasonable annual fees and great rewards structures, and they’re very well rounded:

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card has a $250 annual fee, and offers some solid bonus categories, plus 1,000 Bonvoy bonus points per stay. The card also offers Bonvoy Gold Elite status, 15 elite nights annually for being a cardmember, and a free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

Ultimately, I’d say this is a pretty weak card, especially compared to the rest of Marriott’s card portfolio. It doesn’t offer statement credits or an automatic free night award to offset the annual fee, and you can’t even spend your way to a higher status level on this card. Personally, I’d much rather get the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card or Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, as I think the cards represent a better overall value.

What do you make of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card?

Many airlines, hotels, theme parks and cruise lines pay year-round tribute to military service members with generous discounts and benefits. Sometimes these deals are available only to active-duty military personnel, and at other times the perks extend to U.S. military veterans and their families.

Related: The best credit cards for active-duty military members: Get waived annual fees

No matter the form these military travel deals take, they all reflect the gratitude the travel industry feels toward those who have sacrificed so much to protect our country.

Here are the perks that military members can take advantage of on their travels in 2026.

To honor military members, B Hotels & Resorts offers an exclusive “B Saluted” discount of 15% off regular rates for military members, veterans and their families. Florida-based B Hotels & Resorts has locations in Fort Lauderdale and Marathon.

Through the "Honoring Our Heroes" program, Sandals and Beaches resorts in Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Antigua, the Bahamas, Grenada, Barbados, Curacao, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines offer a 10% discount to eligible U.S. military members and veterans.

Best Western properties across the U.S. offer discounted rates for veterans, military members and government personnel.

Best Western’s Service Rewards program — the hotel chain’s free award program tailored to military and armed forces members — unlocks even more member benefits, including an automatic upgrade to Gold status and bonus points on qualified stays.

In November, military members can receive 10% off their stay at Big Cedar Lodge, as well as 25% off resort activities including a spa day pass, golf simulators, bowling and more.

Through the Waves4Warriors Club, CheapCaribbean Vacations offers active-duty service members, veterans and military families access to exclusive deals, room upgrades, special perks and savings of $150 off a qualifying five-night or longer vacation package after you join at hotel brands including Breathless, Dreams, Zoetry, Royalton and more.

Choice Hotels — including Comfort, Sleep Inn and Quality Inn hotels — offers discounted rates for official and leisure travel to active-duty and retired military personnel, their dependents and members of several military associations. When you are searching for a hotel, open the drop-down "Rate" menu and choose "Military/Veterans (Leisure)" for leisure travel or "Government/Military (Official Business Travel)" for work travel.

Active-duty military members, veterans and military spouses are eligible to join the Choice Privileges rewards program at the Gold Elite level.

Extended Stay America offers discounted rates to military members at three brands and more than 650 locations across the U.S. To receive the discount, choose "Government & Military" from the dropdown box during booking.

Great Wolf Lodge offers up to 40% off nightly rates for active, retired and veteran military members through the Howling Heroes offer. The offer is valid for up to two guests per room, with a $20 fee per additional guest.

The Grove Resort & Water Park is a one-stop hotel and water park only a short drive from Walt Disney World. Military members can receive up to 20% off the best available rate when booking through this link.

Federal and U.S. military employees qualify for military rates and discounts at participating Hilton properties. There are separate discounts for official and leisure military travel. For official military travel, check the box labeled “Government and military rates” to apply the rates. For leisure travel, visit Hilton's Military Family Rate page and search for your travel destination and dates.

Veterans, active-duty members and their immediate family members are eligible for a discount of 10%-15% off Hyatt’s standard rate at participating U.S. hotels. To get the discount, use the offer code "MILVET" while booking.

The hotel chain behind brands such as InterContinental, Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza and Kimpton offers a military rate at participating locations worldwide. The rate applies to active-duty military personnel, veterans, retired military personnel and their families.

Margaritaville Beach Resort's "Salute to Heroes" rate offers up to a 35% discount to active-duty service members and veterans.

Marriott Bonvoy offers discounted federal, state and local government rates available to government and military personnel. To access the discounted rates, choose the “Government & Military” option from the “Special Rates” drop-down menu when searching for a stay. You’ll get a list of all the Marriott Bonvoy properties in your chosen city that offer special rates and their eligibility requirements.

Motel 6, along with its sister extended-stay brand Studio 6, offers a 10% discount on standard rates to active and retired military personnel.

Active-duty military personnel, veterans and government employees are eligible for a 10% discount on official travel at any U.S. Red Roof location. The hotel chain also has a 10% discount on leisure travel for all government employees and military members, veterans and retirees.

If you are traveling to Hawaii for military business or leisure, The Surfjack offers a range of military discounts. With the "Get Shacked @ The Jack" promotion, military members can save 25% on room rates, bring a pet for free and receive discounts on dining and parking.

TradeWinds Resort in St. Pete Beach, Florida, offers up to 25% off its best available rates to military members when you use code "Military" at booking.

Participating Wyndham properties offer discounts of up to 15% off their best available rate to active and retired military personnel, veterans and their families. Plus, qualifying military personnel and their spouses get automatic Gold status when they enroll in the Wyndham Rewards program and bonus Wyndham Rewards points for qualified stays.

In some markets, Alaska Airlines offers discounted military fares to active-duty military personnel and their dependents when you call 800-252-7522 to purchase your tickets. The airline also offers discounts through the WeSalute+ program.

Active-duty U.S. military personnel can board early, check up to five bags for free, receive 15% off inflight food purchases and receive complimentary day passes to visit an Alaska Lounge when traveling on official government-sponsored travel. All other active-duty military personnel can purchase a discounted lounge day pass for $40.

U.S. active-duty and reserve military members, military veterans, members of the National Guard and their dependents get up to two pieces of checked baggage for free through the Allegiant Honors program. Also, the airline waives its typical fees for oversized checked baggage, a carry-on bag, getting a boarding pass printed at the airport, bringing a pet on board, seat assignments and change or cancellation fees due to a change in orders or directives. Qualifying service members can also board their flights early.

American Airlines offers government or military fares in some markets, but you must call the airline at 800-433-7300 to book. Veterans and their families can access reduced fares by enrolling in the WeSalute+ program.

Active-duty military personnel are also allowed Group 1 boarding privileges, and they can bring up to five free checked bags when traveling on orders and up to three free checked bags when traveling for leisure (weight restrictions apply).

U.S. military personnel traveling in uniform on a same-day American flight can enter Admirals Club lounges with their immediate family — defined as a spouse, domestic partner and/or children under 18 — or up to two guests at most Admirals Club locations except for Airspace Lounge at San Diego International Airport (SAN) and Japan Airlines' Sakura Lounge at Honolulu’s Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL).

Active-duty U.S. service members can call Delta Reservations at 800-221-1212 for discounted fares unavailable to the general public. Delta also offers priority boarding and free checked baggage to active-duty military members. The number of bags you are allowed depends on the type of travel and fare type, and you must adhere to the specified baggage size and weight restrictions.

Frontier typically charges for carry-on bags and checked baggage. However, active-duty armed forces, National Guard and Reserve members, their accompanying spouse and children can receive a free carry-on bag, two free checked bags and one free personal item.

Active-duty military personnel traveling for business or leisure are eligible for a 5% discount on base fares. If traveling on government-sponsored business, call 800-538-2583 to receive your discount and up to five free checked bags (military members traveling for leisure get up to two free checked bags). This discount applies to you and your immediate family.

U.S. active-duty military members, retired military members, veterans, National Guard and Reserve members, and their families enrolled in WeSalute+ can also get a 5% discount on base fares and up to two free checked bags.

Special fares are available for military and government travelers, but you must call the airline at 800-435-9792 or visit the airport ticket counter to book them. Additionally, military members traveling on active duty receive priority boarding before Group 1 and are exempt from the two-piece baggage limit.

United offers an additional checked baggage allowance, priority boarding and United Club lounge access to active-duty military members traveling in uniform. U.S. military veterans, active-duty military members, National Guard and Reserve members, and their families are also eligible for a 5% discount on United-operated flights.

Active-duty U.S. military personnel, spouses and dependents are eligible for a 10% discount on the lowest available fare in select fare classes. Select “Military” for each eligible passenger during your ticket search on Fare Finder. Amtrak also welcomes uniformed military personnel to the front of the ticket line.

All U.S. SeaWorld, Busch Gardens, Aquatica and Sesame Place parks offer discounted tickets to active-duty military members and veterans through the Waves of Honor program. Most parks also offer at least one complimentary admission per year.

Disneyland honors active and retired U.S. military personnel with discounted one-, three- and four-day Disney Military Promotional tickets. The three- and four-day tickets include access to Disneyland and Disney California Adventure each day of your ticket, while the one-day ticket is good for entry to one park only (excluding blackout dates). Pricing starts at $98, and you must purchase tickets at a participating U.S. military base ticket office or through govx.com. Theme park reservations are required.

Hotel discounts are also available by calling 866-309-9737.

Dollywood offers discounted tickets and annual passes to U.S. active or retired military members, veterans, military reservists, spouses and dependents.

Military members who visit the home of America's first president can save $4 on admission tickets, while Purple Heart recipients and active-duty members in uniform receive free admission all year long. Every year on Veterans Day, however, all active-duty, former or retired military personnel receive free admission and can participate in an annual tribute by placing a flower on General Washington's tomb.

Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, offers discounted daily tickets and season passes to active, retired and veteran military members. To access this discount, purchase online or present your government ID at the park's ticket booth.

Most U.S.-based Merlin Entertainments attractions offer discounted military tickets, but a handful of locations are giving away free tickets to military members and veterans through Nov. 30. These include Legoland parks in Florida and New York, Madame Tussauds Orlando and Sea Life Aquariums in Orlando, Grapevine, Texas, Kansas City, Missouri, and San Antonio, Texas.

Active duty and retired military personnel and veterans, along with their spouses and dependents, can purchase a Military Passport season pass starting at $119.99.Silver Dollar City also offers a ticket discount to U.S. active or retired military personnel, veterans and military reservists, along with their spouses and dependent children (ages 4-17) living in their households.

In addition to discounted tickets, Silver Dollar City invites all military members and veterans to help raise the American flag during the park’s daily opening ceremony. Service members are also given a red, white and blue ribbon to wear in the park, allowing employees and guests to thank them for their service.

St. Augustine has hundreds of years of military history, much of which you can still visit today. The city shows its appreciation to military service members year-round with discounts on accommodations, attractions and experiences.

Universal Orlando offers a Military Freedom Pass promotional ticket to all active-duty and retired service members. Ticket prices start at $220 for unlimited admission between now and Dec.18, 2026, though blackout dates apply. Each eligible service member can purchase up to six promotional tickets and must buy them through a participating authorized military ticket and travel office. Military members can also purchase discounted tickets to the new Universal Epic Universe park.

Universal Studios Hollywood offers discounted tickets to active-duty, retired and eligible veteran military members, along with their spouses and dependents. Additional on-base discounts are available, including a 12-month Military Pass.

Active and retired U.S. military personnel are eligible for discounted hotel rates and specially priced theme park tickets at Walt Disney World. Military members can purchase a Military Salute ticket with either Park Hopper or Park Hopper Plus starting at $409 for a four-day ticket, $429 for a five-day ticket and $449 for a six-day ticket. Disney World also offers a special ticket valid for multiple visits through Dec. 18, 2026, starting at $499.

Blackout dates apply, and theme park reservations are required. Hotel stays can be booked by calling 407-939-7830. Tickets must be purchased at a participating U.S. military base ticket office to avoid being charged a sales tax, but are also available at Disney World ticket windows.

Vail Resorts offers Epic Military Passes for active-duty service members, retired military members and veterans. Prices start at just $230 for unlimited skiing at more than 40 Vail Resorts and discounts on family passes, food, lodging, gear rentals and more.

AmaWaterways offers active and retired service members a special military discount of $250 per person off a river cruise or enjoy two-for-one cruise fares on select 2026 and 2027 sailings when you use the code "MIL250" or "MIL2FOR1" when booking.

Carnival Cruise Line shows its appreciation for active and retired members of the armed forces with discounted cruise rates, onboard credits and reduced deposits. Additionally, some ships have a Heroes Tribute Lounge, and every ship holds a military appreciation gathering for service members and their families.

On select Celebrity Cruises sailings, active and retired military members can save $25 on inside and ocean-view cabins and $100 on veranda cabins and above, and these savings can be combined with other current promotions. This discount applies to the first and second guests in the cabin.

Disney Cruise Line offers special rates to all military members, active and retired, and their spouses. Discounted rates are only available on select sailings. To honor America's 250th anniversary, the cruise line is offering a $250 onboard credit for eligible U.S. military personnel on select Disney Wish and Disney Dream sailings in 2026.

MSC Cruises offers discounted fares to all active and retired U.S. military personnel, as well as family members traveling with them. You can receive a discount of 5% on interior and ocean-view cabins, 10% on balcony and suite cabins, and a “kids sail free” promotion on select sailings.

Margaritaville at Sea honors active and veteran military members with a free cruise through the Heroes Sail Free program. On select sailings, military members and an additional guest in the same cabin can get a free fare (taxes and fees are not included). A third and fourth guest can be added at the regular fare. On all other sailings, military members can save 20% off the retail fare for the first four guests in the cabin.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Military Appreciation program extends exclusive benefits to military members, veterans and their spouses. Members of the program receive up to a 20% discount on select sailings.

Veterans and active, retired and disabled military personnel can receive up to $250 free onboard spending money on select Princess Cruises sailings. You can use this onboard credit for specialty dining, onboard boutiques, shore excursions, spa treatments and more.

Royal Caribbean offers military rates to active and retired personnel, veterans and their spouses. The discounted rates also apply to friends and family members staying in the same cabin as the eligible service member. The best way to access the discounted rate is to book through a travel agent or to book directly with Royal Caribbean over the phone.

A host of benefits awaits travelers who have served or are serving in the U.S. military.

Because these military travel deals, their requirements, and the eligibility of family members, spouses and dependents vary, carefully research each military discount offer to avoid surprises. Many airlines, hotels and other businesses might ask for proof of eligibility, so don’t leave home without the military ID, veteran ID, dependent ID, orders and/or other documentation you’ll need to take advantage of the many travel offers.
